title: Slow First, Fast Later: Temporal Speed‐Up in Service Episodes of Finite Duration
abstract: Many service environments such as outpatient departments comprise repeated episodes of finite duration wherein customers arriving during an episode must be served before the end of that episode. Scheduling resources and customer arrivals in such settings involves trading off customer wait against resources’ time and effort. We hypothesize that this trade‐off leads to a “slow first, fast later” pattern of system speed, which allows build‐up of inventory earlier for more efficient utilization of faster system speed later. As a natural corollary, we also hypothesize that greater anticipated workload, which causes faster inventory build‐up, leads to a larger increase in system speed earlier in the service episode than later. We empirically validate these hypotheses using operational data from a high volume tertiary care outpatient department. Our estimation results suggest that due to hypothesized system speed pattern, patients arriving around the middle (later) part of the episode experience 20% (63%) shorter length of stay compared to those arriving at the beginning. Further, additional anticipated workload of 1 patient per hour leads to 14%, 4%, and negligible reduction in the average length of stay during the earlier, middle, and later part of the service episode, respectively. Counterfactual simulations based on our model estimates show that “slow first, fast later” system speed pattern yields faster completion of work as compared to an equivalent constant system speed pattern.

summary.oneLiner: Outpatient data suggest a "slow first, fast later" speed pattern: patients arriving mid-episode see shorter stays, and total work finishes sooner.
summary.overview: Many services, such as hospital outpatient clinics, run in repeated sessions that end at a fixed time, and every customer who arrives during a session must be served before it closes. The authors argue that staff speed should vary within each session: they work more slowly early on, which lets a backlog of patients build up, and then work faster later to clear that backlog. Using operational data from a high-volume tertiary care outpatient department (a large specialist hospital clinic), they find that patients arriving mid-session or later have much shorter stays than those arriving at the start. They also find that a higher expected workload speeds up the early-session change more than the later one, and simulations based on their estimates suggest this pattern finishes work faster than a constant speed.
summary.question: Does system speed follow a "slow first, fast later" pattern within finite-duration service episodes, and does greater anticipated workload make the speed increase larger earlier in the episode than later?
summary.method: The authors estimate a model on operational data to test two hypotheses: the "slow first, fast later" speed pattern and a larger early-episode speed response to anticipated workload. They then run counterfactual simulations based on the model estimates to compare this speed pattern with a constant speed.
summary.data: Operational data from a high-volume tertiary care outpatient department. The time period is not stated in the available text.
findings: Estimation results suggest that, due to the hypothesized system speed pattern, patients arriving around the middle of the episode experience about 20% shorter length of stay than those arriving at the beginning.
Patients arriving in the later part of the episode experience about 63% shorter length of stay than those arriving at the beginning.

Additional anticipated workload of 1 patient per hour is associated with about 14%, 4%, and negligible reductions in average length of stay during the earlier, middle, and later parts of the episode, respectively.
Counterfactual simulations based on the model estimates show that the "slow first, fast later" pattern yields faster completion of work than an equivalent constant system speed.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors frame the findings as a trade-off between customer wait and the time and effort of resources in scheduling both staff and arrivals within service episodes. They suggest that building up a queue early allows more efficient use of faster speed later, which may matter for managers scheduling outpatient or similar episodic services. The paper's abstract does not state explicit policy recommendations.
industries: Healthcare (outpatient department of a tertiary care hospital)
